endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Important to note, KPNC instituted a mandatory two-week shadowing period before each hospital's go-live, during which alerts were shown to selected clinicians for workflow practice runs (functioning as a simulation environment where staff could rehearse the system before patient safety was at stake).

evidence.title: Tackling alert fatigue with a semi-automated clinical decision support system: quantitative evaluation and end-user survey
evidence.outcome: Physician alert burden and acceptance with clinical pharmacist review of alerts
evidence.effect: Of 10,556 alerts, 619 went directly to physicians and 2,231 after pharmacist review; pharmacists received 17.2 alerts/day vs 7.8 notifications/day for all physicians; acceptance 89.8% (direct) and 68.4% (pharmacist-reviewed), 72.4% overall.
evidence.quote: Involving clinical pharmacists proved a promising approach to limit the alert burden of physicians and thus tackle alert fatigue.

evidence.title: Guiding Clostridioides difficile Infection Prevention Efforts in a Hospital Setting With AI
evidence.outcome: Clinician response to AI-triggered best practice advisory alerts
evidence.effect: Of 17 practitioners interviewed, 6 tended to ignore the BPAs and 10 could not recall BPA content, despite only 1-2 study BPAs per week.
evidence.quote: Of the 17 primary inpatient practitioners interviewed, 6 indicated that they tended to ignore the BPAs and 10 could not recall the BPA content.

evidence.title: Computer-Aided Colonoscopy Alert Fatigue and Its Effect on Adenoma Detection
evidence.outcome: Alert fatigue reducing CADe effectiveness through the day
evidence.effect: CADe-assisted ADR fell from 49.9% in first 3 procedures to 39.9% in later procedures; ADR gain per WT minute 10.5% early vs 10.1% late.
evidence.quote: This pattern suggests that alert fatigue may limit endoscopists' responsiveness to CADe prompts as the day progresses.

evidence.title: Evaluation of sepsis CDS tool knowledge and utilization among graduate medical trainees: insights to inform redesign in an academic health system
evidence.outcome: Trainee-reported alert fatigue with EHR sepsis alert
evidence.effect: Alert fatigue (62.5%) and limited clinical utility (46.3%) were major concerns among 80 trainees who recognized the sepsis alert.
evidence.quote: Alert fatigue (62.5%) and limited clinical utility (46.3%) were major concerns.

evidence.title: Healthcare Professionals' Expectations of Medical Artificial Intelligence and Strategies for its Clinical Implementation: A Qualitative Study
evidence.outcome: Clinician concerns about alert fatigue from medical AI in ER/ICU settings
evidence.effect: Participants raised alert fatigue as a concern about medical AI. The authors highlighted alert fatigue management as important. No frequency was reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: They also highlighted the importance of alert fatigue management and the integration of AI systems into the workflow.

commentary.bottom_line: One descriptive study from a Swiss hospital found that clinical pharmacists screening 10,556 alerts passed 2,231 to physicians after review, and physicians accepted 68.4% of those reviewed alerts. No study tested remote nurses as the intermediary, and the one test does not state whether its alerts came from an AI system.

perspectives.view: The only test is a cross-sectional study. It examined clinical pharmacist review rather than remote nurses, and its summary does not state whether the alerts came from an AI system, which limits directness. Four hazard studies show alert fatigue exists but do not test intermediary review. The CHAI endorsement describes pre-go-live shadowing, not an intermediary team. Certainty is very low.

In the pharmacist study, physicians accepted 89.8% of direct alerts and 68.4% of reviewed alerts. The summary does not report whether filtered-out alerts included true risks or whether patient harm changed. The hazard is documented. In one AI deployment, 6 of 17 practitioners tended to ignore advisories and 10 could not recall their content.

Pharmacists received 17.2 alerts per day, compared with 7.8 notifications per day for all physicians. This suggests that the burden moves to the reviewing team rather than disappearing. Adenoma detection with computer-aided detection fell from 49.9% to 39.9% in later procedures. That finding suggests a reviewing team may also be exposed to fatigue.

The one deployment relied on pharmacists handling 17.2 alerts per day. A health system would need dedicated reviewer time and a way to hand off urgent findings. No study reported costs, staffing models, or results for remote nurse teams, so feasibility at scale has not been tested.

The single test took place in Switzerland, and its summary does not describe the payer mix, language, or literacy of the patients. The summaries of the hazard studies from the United States, Canada, and South Korea also report no subgroup data. Evidence on which patients benefit or lose when alerts are filtered is absent.

commentary.research_gap: Comparative studies are needed that place remote nurses or other intermediary teams between confirmed AI alerts and frontline clinicians. These studies should measure missed true-positive alerts, time to clinical response, reviewer fatigue, patient outcomes, staffing costs, and results by patient subgroup.
commentary.underserved_note: No test reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The only test came from a Swiss hospital and did not report patient characteristics in its summary. Health systems serving these populations cannot tell from current evidence whether intermediary review helps or harms their patients.
